p01.why: The default argument's temporary belongs to the full expression of the call, so it ends before the next statement writes 9.

p02.why: Two unsequenced reads of a volatile object are undefined, but the Evidence says no compiler diagnoses them and the program has no main.

p03.why: The operands of built-in * have an unspecified order and the calls do not interleave, so either order passes the check.

p04.why: A member operator- has an unspecified operand order and the program accepts both orders.

p05.why: For a.*b the object is evaluated before the member pointer.

p06.why: The two calls do not overlap, so they return 0 and 1 in some order and the sum is 1.

p07.why: An overloaded ->* keeps the built-in order, object first.

p08.why: Plain sequential statements in a constexpr function; the static_assert holds and there is no main.

p09.why: Operator notation keeps the shift order, and the explicit call accepts either order.

p10.why: The argument's side effect is complete before the body runs, so the body sees g == 1 and returns 10.

p11.why: Arguments are evaluated whole in an unspecified order, so r is 1 or 10 and i is 2.

p12.why: In a[b] the array operand comes first.

p13.why: A reversed comparison candidate has an unspecified operand order and both orders pass.

p14.why: Indeterminately sequenced arguments give pair(0,1) or pair(0,0); both pass.

p15.why: An overloaded += keeps the assignment order, so the right operand is evaluated first.

p16.why: Two unsequenced writes to count; no sanitizer or flag stops it.

p17.why: An overloaded << keeps the shift order, left to right.

p18.why: The function expression is evaluated before the arguments.

p19.why: Argument order is unspecified and the program accepts both orders.

p20.why: Assignment evaluates the right operand first, so z, then y, then x.

p21.why: The object expression of a member call is part of the function and comes before the arguments.

p22.why: Built-in & has an unspecified operand order and both orders pass.

p23.why: Elements of a braced list are evaluated in order, so a is 0 and b is 1.

p24.why: i + i++ is an unsequenced read and write; Clang and GCC warn and -Werror makes the warning an error (EDG skips the test).

p25.why: The copy into self, the copy into the second parameter, and next() each add 1, in any order, so count is 3.

p26.why: An overloaded [] keeps the subscript order, table first.

p27.why: An overloaded = keeps the assignment order, right operand first.

p28.why: Built-in compound assignment evaluates the right operand first.

p29.why: Each operand of op=, ++ and -- is evaluated once, the structured binding, range and switch condition are evaluated once, so 610 and 3312 hold at translation and at run time.

p30.why: i++ + i++ makes Clang and GCC warn about unsequenced modifications, and -Werror rejects it.

p31.why: The right side of the assignment is complete before the write, so i is 2 and j is 3.

p32.why: The right side reads i (0) before the left side increments it, so cells[0] becomes 0.

p33.why: Built-in < has an unspecified order and both orders pass.

p34.why: An unsequenced write and read of i in the operands of *.

p35.why: Adjacent bit-fields share a memory location, so the call would be undefined, but the compilers do not warn and there is no main.

p36.why: Each compound assignment and increment calls at() once, and the range expression is evaluated once.

p37.why: Each listed construct calls the counted function the stated number of times.

p38.why: Each full expression completes before the next.

p39.why: The prvalue initializes the exception object directly, so two constructors and two destructors give 4, and the overloaded ~ adds 1.

p40.why: The explicit and default arguments are evaluated in an unspecified order and the program accepts both.
